title: Berabbi
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: We find a Tanna of a baraita called Berabbi, as in [Makkot 5b](https://www.sefaria.org/Makkot.5b.10): “Berabbi taught: If they did not kill, they are killed,” and Rashi explains that this was his name. In [Chullin 11b:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.11b.8) [Rashi on Chullin 11b:8:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Chullin.11b.8.2) explains: we do not know who he is, but [he was] one great in his generation. In [Chullin 52b:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.52b.15): “Berabbi taught: They did not say ‘mauled’,” etc., and [Rashi on Chullin 52b:15:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Chullin.52b.15.1) explains: the name of a sage.

Apart from these three places, we find the title Berabbi with a personal name, such as Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, who is also called Rabban Gamliel Berabbi, as in [Shabbat 115a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.115a.7) and [Shabbat 151b:14](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.151b.14) and [Kiddushin 32b:4-6](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.32b.4-6), and Hyman reads [Rashi on Kiddushin 32b:5:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Kiddushin.32b.5.2) as describing a great man rather than Rabbi’s son. Likewise Rabban Gamliel, the son of Rabbi, as in Jerusalem Talmud Challah 4:4, and Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah Nesia, as in Jerusalem Talmud Avodah Zarah 1:1. They also called Rabbi Yose ben Chalafta Berabbi, as in [Sukkah 26a:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.26a.7), and [Rashi on Sukkah 26a:7:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Sukkah.26a.7.1) explains: Yose the sage, the sharpest in his generation; and in [Pesachim 100a:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.100a.7) Hyman attributes to Rashi the explanation that Berabbi means a great man and that it describes Rabbi Yose as the great sage of his generation. In the consulted edition this is [Rashbam on Pesachim 100a:7:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashbam_on_Pesachim.100a.7.2).[^4]

Hyman says that Rabbi Elazar HaKappar is always called Berabbi, as in [Chullin 28a:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.28a.3) and [Chullin 84b:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.84b.8) and [Avodah Zarah 43a:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.43a.7). Hyman cites Berakhot 24b: “Rabbi Yochanan said: Achai Berabbi,” and Rashi explains: great in his generation, and wherever it says Berabbi this is its meaning. In [Eruvin 53a:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.53a.12) Rabbi Yochanan called Rabbi Oshaya his teacher “Berabbi.”[^5]
In [Kiddushin 80b:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.80b.3) Rabbi Yochanan called Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, when he heard this, “Berabbi.”

In [Chullin 57a:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.57a.6) Rabbi Yose bar Chanina called Chizkiyah “Berabbi,” and [Rashi on Chullin 57a:6:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Chullin.57a.6.1) explains that he was great in his generation. In Jerusalem Talmud Bikkurim 3:3 Rabbi Yannai called Yehudah son of Rabbi Chiyya, his son-in-law, “Yehudah Berabbi”; likewise in Shabbat, beginning of halakhah 2 of chapter 7, “Rabbi Sidor said: Yehudah Berabbi”; in Bava Batra, chapter 5, end of halakhah 4, “Rabbi La in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Berabbi”; Bereshit Rabbah 37:6 and 91:11, “Yehudah Berabbi”; and in Yoma 2:1, folio 8b, a dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehudah Berabbi. Likewise in Rosh Hashanah 1:1, “Yehudah bei Rabbi said: A large account swallows a small account,” and Hyman proposes “Yehudah Berabbi.”

In [Kiddushin 21b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.21b.7) and Bekhorot 33b, “Yudan Berabbi used to expound,” and Rashi explains: Yudan was his name, and he was great in his generation; wherever they call him Berabbi it is an expression of wisdom and sharpness. In Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 10:1 Rabbi Yose called Rabbi Simon “Berabbi.” After examination Hyman suggests that wherever the title Berabbi is mentioned with a personal name it should be written ברבי without a yod, and wherever it is [the person’s] name it should be בריבי with a yod. He reports examining all the places where it is mentioned with a personal name and finding them mostly without the yod, and in a few places with the yod, where Dikdukei Soferim reads without the yod. In the Responsa Noda BiYehudah, second edition, Orach Chayim, siman 113, it is cited that the Gaon Rabbi Yeshayah Pik asked him about this.[^3][^6]

notes.text: The final סקי״ג is siman113, not13. The Hebrew ברבי/בריבי difference is explicitly retained even though the English label is shared; Hyman’s proposed distinction between an honorific and a personal name remains his own rule. ואך היה שמו is read as his name, ובברוכות as Berakhot; all full personal names and differing sources remain separate, without blanket son-of-Rabbi expansion.

The consulted Makkot 5b reads Beribbi’s statement about the witnesses, followed by his father’s question; Rashi there glosses that this was his name. This supports that occurrence, not a single identity for every occurrence or Hyman’s general distinction between ברבי as an honorific and בריבי as a personal name. His always and wherever formulations remain his own claims. The supplied Noda BiYehudah pointer is second edition, Orach Chayim 113; that exact printing and the claimed Dikdukei Soferim spellings have not been independently inspected here. The differing named bearers are not merged or all expanded as sons of Rabbi.

In Makkot Rashi takes Beribi as the speaker’s name. The linked Shabbat and Kiddushin passages show the form beside a personal name or title. Hyman’s proposed spelling distinction remains his interpretation. See also [Rashi’s name gloss](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Makkot.5b.10.1).

At [Chullin 11b:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.11b.8), Rashi takes the unnamed speaker to be a distinguished sage of his generation. In [Chullin 52b:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.52b.15), Rashi glosses the word as a sage’s name. At [Shabbat 151b:14](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.151b.14), the Hebrew has Rabbi Gamliel Berabbi; the consulted English identifies him as the son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi. At [Kiddushin 80b:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.80b.3), the Hebrew has Berabbi without a personal name, and [Rashi on Kiddushin 80b:3:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Kiddushin.80b.3.1) identifies him as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. The occurrences do not use the title in the same way.

In [Bekhorot 24b:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.24b.1), Achai Berabbi asks about an animal that follows a ewe. [Rashi on Bekhorot 24b:1:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Bekhorot.24b.1.1) explains the title as a great and distinguished man of his generation. The consulted passage introduces Achai’s question without the Rabbi Yochanan attribution given by Hyman.

The earlobe teaching at [Bekhorot 37b:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.37b.12) also has “Yudan Berabbi used to expound.” Hyman cites Bekhorot 33b. [Rashi on Bekhorot 37b:12:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Bekhorot.37b.12.1) glosses Berabbi as “a great man.”
